Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem

When does a family of continuous functions hide a uniformly convergent subsequence? Uniform boundedness plus equicontinuity lets the diagonal argument extract one. Contrast with xnx^nxn, where it fails.

F⊂C(K) relatively compactF \subset C(K)\ \text{relatively compact}F⊂C(K) relatively compact
  ⟺  uniformly bounded+equicontinuous\iff \text{uniformly bounded} + \text{equicontinuous}⟺uniformly bounded+equicontinuous

Examples & Exercises

Let KKK be a compact metric space and F⊂C(K)F \subset C(K)F⊂C(K) relatively compact in the sup norm. Prove FFF is equicontinuous using a finite ε/3\varepsilon/3ε/3-net (hint: each net member is uniformly continuous on the compact KKK).

  5. Note: only pointwise boundedness was used here. Upgrading this pointwise convergence to uniform convergence on all of KKK is the job of equicontinuity, carried out by the ε/3\varepsilon/3ε/3 argument in the next problem.

Let (fn)⊂C(K)(f_n) \subset C(K)(fn​)⊂C(K) be equicontinuous and pointwise bounded (KKK compact metric), converging pointwise on a countable dense set {xk}\{x_k\}{xk​}. Prove by the ε/3\varepsilon/3ε/3 argument that the convergence is uniform on all of KKK, and deduce as a corollary that (xn)(x^n)(xn) has no uniformly convergent subsequence on [0,1][0,1][0,1].

∣fmj(x)−fmℓ(x)∣≤ε3+ε3+ε3=ε(uniformly Cauchy)\lvert f_{m_j}(x) - f_{m_\ell}(x) \rvert \le \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon \quad \text{(uniformly Cauchy)}∣fmj​​(x)−fmℓ​​(x)∣≤3ε​+3ε​+3ε​=ε(uniformly Cauchy)
xn→{0x∈[0,1)1x=1(discontinuous pointwise limit)x^n \to \begin{cases} 0 & x \in [0, 1) \\ 1 & x = 1 \end{cases} \quad \text{(discontinuous pointwise limit)}xn→{01​x∈[0,1)x=1​(discontinuous pointwise limit)
Show proof
  1. Given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, equicontinuity yields δ>0\delta > 0δ>0: d(x,y)<δd(x, y) < \deltad(x,y)<δ implies ∣fn(x)−fn(y)∣<ε/3\lvert f_n(x) - f_n(y) \rvert < \varepsilon/3∣fn​(x)−fn​(y)∣<ε/3 for every nnn. Since KKK is compact, finitely many points xk1,…,xkrx_{k_1}, \dots, x_{k_r}xk1​​,…,xkr​​ from the dense set {xk}\{x_k\}{xk​} form a δ\deltaδ-net of KKK.
  2. At the finitely many net points, pointwise convergence becomes "uniform": choose NNN so large that j,ℓ≥Nj, \ell \ge Nj,ℓ≥N gives ∣fmj(xki)−fmℓ(xki)∣<ε/3\lvert f_{m_j}(x_{k_i}) - f_{m_\ell}(x_{k_i}) \rvert < \varepsilon/3∣fmj​​(xki​​)−fmℓ​​(xki​​)∣<ε/3 for every iii (a finite intersection of tails).
  3. For arbitrary x∈Kx \in Kx∈K, pick xkix_{k_i}xki​​ with d(x,xki)<δd(x, x_{k_i}) < \deltad(x,xki​​)<δ. By the triangle inequality, ∣fmj(x)−fmℓ(x)∣≤∣fmj(x)−fmj(xki)∣+∣fmj(xki)−fmℓ(xki)∣+∣fmℓ(xki)−fmℓ(x)∣<ε/3+ε/3+ε/3=ε\lvert f_{m_j}(x) - f_{m_\ell}(x) \rvert \le \lvert f_{m_j}(x) - f_{m_j}(x_{k_i}) \rvert + \lvert f_{m_j}(x_{k_i}) - f_{m_\ell}(x_{k_i}) \rvert + \lvert f_{m_\ell}(x_{k_i}) - f_{m_\ell}(x) \rvert < \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon∣fmj​​(x)−fmℓ​​(x)∣≤∣fmj​​(x)−fmj​​(xki​​)∣+∣fmj​​(xki​​)−fmℓ​​(xki​​)∣+∣fmℓ​​(xki​​)−fmℓ​​(x)∣<ε/3+ε/3+ε/3=ε. Hence (fmj)(f_{m_j})(fmj​​) is uniformly Cauchy, so it converges uniformly by completeness of C(K)C(K)C(K).
  4. This completes (⟸\Longleftarrow⟸): pointwise bounded + equicontinuous implies uniformly bounded (as noted in the first problem), and every sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence, so by sequential compactness in metric spaces the set is relatively compact.
  5. Corollary: (xn)(x^n)(xn) has no uniformly convergent subsequence on [0,1][0,1][0,1]. Its pointwise limit is discontinuous — 0 on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1), 1 at x=1x = 1x=1. If some subsequence converged uniformly, its limit would be continuous (a uniform limit of continuous functions) and would have to equal the pointwise limit — contradiction. So {xn}\{x^n\}{xn} is not equicontinuous at x=1x = 1x=1: as the scene's contrast chart shows, pairwise sup distances between distinct members stay at least 0.47 apart.
